rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison leaves its counterpart unstated: one whose heart Allah hardened; the following warning about hard hearts makes the omission clear.
rows.anchor: أفمن شرح الله صدره للإسلام كمن أقسى قلبه فحذف لدلالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “ما قلى,” the object is omitted to preserve the verse endings in alif.
rows.anchor: فحذف المفعول لأن فواصل الآي على الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Objects of شاء are often omitted when their content is implied by the answer; the estimate is “if God willed to do that, He would.”
rows.anchor: والحكمة في كثرة حذف مفعول المشيئة المستلزمة لمضمون الجواب

rows.speaker: ابن النحوية
rows.claim: Ibn al-Nahwiyya conditions omission of the object on a conditional particle preceding it.
rows.anchor: وشرط ابن النحوية 5 في حذفه دخول أداة الشرط عليه كما سبق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Zamalkani, and al-Tanukhi allow regular omission of the object of إرادة as with مشيئة; the response supplies its implied content.
rows.anchor: صرح به الزمخشري في تفسير سورة البقرة وابن الزملكاني في البرهان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In يريدون ليطفئوا, the intended object is omitted because the previous verse already says they were charged with their supposed aim; the later phrase clarifies it and heightens its unusual character.
rows.anchor: لأن في الآية قبلها ما يدل على أنهم أمروا لكذب

rows.speaker: عبد القاهر الجرجاني
rows.claim: For “if We had willed, We would have given every soul its guidance,” estimate the object as willing to give each soul guidance; otherwise the conditional would imply that God has no will at all.
rows.anchor: كما قاله عبد القاهر الجرجاني ولو شئنا أن نؤتي كل نفس هداها لآتيناها

rows.speaker: النحويون
rows.claim: For “if We had willed, We would have raised him by it,” grammarians estimate: We did not will it, so We did not raise him.
rows.anchor: فقدره النحويون فلم نشأ فلم نرفعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari alternates between placing the interrogative hamza before a conjunction and making it govern an omitted clause; the author prefers the hamza before the conjunction.
rows.anchor: وتارة يجعلها متقدمة على العاطف كما ذكرناه وهو الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted-verb analysis cannot work in examples such as “أو من ينشأ في الحلية,” “أفمن يعلم,” and “أفمن هو قائم.”
rows.anchor: لا يمكن فيها تقدير فعل قبلها كقوله تعالى ﴿ أو من ينشأ في الحلية ﴾

rows.speaker: ابن خطيب زملكا
rows.claim: Ibn Khatib Zamlaka says the best parse inserts an omitted clause after the hamza and before fa; “if he dies” then introduces the consequence of reverting after his lifetime.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن خطيب زملكا ( 1 ) الاوجه ان يقدر محذوف بعد الهمزة قبل الفاء

rows.speaker: ابن سيدة
rows.claim: Ibn Sida claims that any verb asked about must refer only to the future.
rows.anchor: زعم ابن سيدة ( 3 ) في كلامه على اثبات الجمل ان كل فعل يستفهم عنه

rows.speaker: الأعلم
rows.claim: Al-Aʿlam rejects Ibn Sida’s rule: questions can concern the past, as in “Did you find what your Lord promised true?” and ordinary past-tense examples.
rows.anchor: ورد عليه الاعلم ( 4 ) وقال هذا باطل ولم يمنع أحد هل قام زيد أمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A conditional construction pairs two clauses, with the first verbal so it suits the condition.
rows.anchor: المجازاة إنما تنعقد بين جملتين أولاهما فعلية لتلائم الشرط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apodosis may be nominal, verbal (jussive or not), adverbial, or itself conditional; joined to the protasis, the first is the condition and the second its answer, also called antecedent and consequent.
rows.anchor: وثانيهما قد تكون اسمية وقد تكون فعلية جازمة وغير جازمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A marfuʿ report divides the Qur’an into seven long suras, the hundred-verse suras, the mathani, and the mufassal, corresponding respectively to the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, and a special gift; it is gharīb and its transmitter Saʿid b. Bashir is weak, though al-Tayalisi also transmits it.
rows.anchor: عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال أعطيت السبع الطول مكان التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seven long suras begin with al-Baqara and end with Bara’a; Anfal and Bara’a were counted as one and not separated because both descended during the Prophet’s campaigns, and they are called long for their length.
rows.anchor: فالسبع الطول أولها البقرة وآخرها براءة لأنهم كانوا يعدون الأنفال وبراءة سورة واحدة

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid b. Jubayr instead counted the seven long suras as al-Baqara through al-Aʿraf, followed by Yunus.
rows.anchor: وحكى عن سعيد بن جبير أنه عد السبع الطول البقرة وآل عمران

rows.speaker: أبو حيان التوحيدي
rows.claim: Al-Tiwal is the plural of tulā, by analogy with kubār from kubrā; Abu Hayyan al-Tawhidi calls pronouncing the first vowel with kasra poor usage.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حيان التوحيدى وكسر الطاء مرذول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The miʾun follow the seven long suras and are named for suras exceeding or approaching one hundred verses.
rows.anchor: والمئون ما ولى السبع الطول سميت بذلك لأن كل سورة منها تزيد على مائة آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mathani follow the miʾun; all Qur’an suras may be called mathani because reports and stories recur, while “the seven mathani” can mean al-Fatiha, repeated in every rakʿa.
rows.anchor: وإنما سمى القرآن كله مثانى لأن الأنباء والقصص تثنى فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mufassal follows the mathani and comprises short suras; its name is explained by frequent basmala divisions between suras or by having little abrogation, and it ends with Surat al-Nas.
rows.anchor: سمى مفصلا لكثرة الفصول التى بين السور ببسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Twelve views are given for the beginning of the mufassal; this passage lists al-Jathiya, Muhammad (attributed by al-Mawardi to most scholars), al-Hujurat, and Qaf, with Qaf tied to a report about the Prophet’s hizb divisions.
rows.anchor: وفى أوله اثنا عشر قولا أحدها الجاثية ثانيها القتال وعزاه الماوردى للأكثرين

rows.speaker: الخطابي
rows.claim: Al-Khattabi cites a report from a Thaqif delegation: the Prophet’s companions divided the Qur’an into hizbs and began the mufassal hizb at Qaf; Ahmad also transmitted it, and al-Mawardi says many Companions related it.
rows.anchor: وفيه حديث ذكره الخطابى فى غريبه يرويه عيسى بن يونس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surahs can have one or several names: examples include al-Baqara as Fustat al-Qur’an, al-Imran as Tayyiba in the Torah, al-Nahl as the sura of favors, al-Shura, al-Shariʿa, and al-Qital.
rows.anchor: قد يكون للسورة اسم وهو كثير وقد يكون لها اسمان كسورة البقرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ma’ida is also called al-ʿUqud and al-Munqitha; Ghafir is also al-Tawl and al-Mu’min, the latter name drawn from “a believing man.”
rows.anchor: وكسورة غافر والطول والمؤمن لقوله ﴿ وقال رجل مؤمن ﴾

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Bara’a is also called al-Tawba, al-Fadiha, and al-Hafira because it exposed hypocrites’ hearts; Ibn Abbas says repeated “and among them” passages made them fear nearly everyone would be named.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس ما زال ينزل ﴿ ومنهم ﴾ حتى ظننا أنه لا يبقى أحد إلا ذكر فيها

rows.speaker: حذيفة
rows.claim: Hudhayfa called Bara’a the sura of punishment; Ibn Umar called it al-Mushaqshiqah; al-Harith b. Yazid says it was called al-Mubaʿthira, and it is also known as al-Masura and al-Buhuth.
rows.anchor: وقال حذيفة هى سورة العذاب وقال ابن عمر كنا ندعوها المشقشقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Fatiha has more than twenty names, including al-Fatiha, Umm al-Kitab, Umm al-Qur’an, the seven mathani, al-Salah, al-Hamd, al-Wafiya, al-Kanz, al-Shafiya, al-Shifa, al-Kafiya, and al-Asas; reports establish several of these titles.
rows.anchor: ذكر بعضهم لها بضعة وعشرين اسما الفاتحة وثبت فى الصحيحين وأم الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author asks whether surah names are fixed by revelation or inferred from apt associations; he finds the latter unlikely, since a clever reader could derive many names from every surah’s meanings.
rows.anchor: وينبغى البحث عن تعداد الأسامى هل هو توقيفى أو بما يظهر من المناسبات

rows.speaker: عامة المتكلمين
rows.claim: Most theologians say all Qur’an must be knowable or its benefit would be lost; they read “the firmly grounded” as coordinated with “Allah” and “they say” as a circumstantial clause, as al-Raghib reports.
rows.anchor: قال الراغب ( 1 ) في مقدمة تفسيره وذهب عامة المتكلمين إلى أن كل القرآن يجب أن يكون معلوما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says revelation has four aspects: lawful and forbidden matters, what none may be ignorant of, what Arabs know, and interpretation known only to God.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس أنزل الله القرآن على أربعة أوجه حلال وحرام

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some distinguish two senses of mutashabih: obscure meaning due to intermingled doubt, whose intent may remain inaccessible unless God graciously reveals it, or mutually confirming passages whose intent people can know.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم المتشابه اسم لمعنيين أحدهما لما التبس من المعنى لدخون شبهة بعضه في بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second sense of mutashabih is that parts agree and confirm one another, as in the description of the Book as mutashabih and mathani.
rows.anchor: والثاني اسم لما يوافق بعضه بعضا ويصدقه قوله تعالى ﴿ كتابا متشابها مثاني ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the ambiguous can be understood, it encourages scholarly inquiry into subtle meanings, prevents unthinking imitation, tests people, and earns reward; clear passages provide a basis for interpreting it, creating effort and merit.
rows.anchor: فلو كان القرآن كله محكما لا يحتاج إلى تأويل لسقطت المحنة وبطل التفاضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Men are qawwamun over women” and “stand for God devoutly” do not conflict: physical standing and upholding a command are different aspects of the act.
rows.anchor: فقيام الانتصاب لا ينافي القيام بالأمر لاختلاف جهتي الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You see people drunk though they are not” and “death comes to him everywhere but he is not dead” differ by respect: drunkenness is figurative relative to Judgment’s terrors, but literal relative to wine.
rows.anchor: وهو يرجع لقول المناطقة الاختلاف بالإضافة أي وترى الناس سكارى بالإضافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Statements that people profess belief without believing, hear without hearing, or look without seeing are compatible because the terms apply in different senses; denying sight does not entail lack of eyesight.
rows.anchor: فإنه لا يلزم من نفي النظر نفي الإبصار لجواز قولهم

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Qutrub reads “your sight today is sharp” as strong knowledge and understanding rather than eyesight, from the usage “aware of something”; al-Farisi adduces the removal of the veil.
rows.anchor: قال قطرب ﴿ فبصرك ﴾ 2 أي علمك ومعرفتك بها قوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Pharaoh says “your gods” yet “I am your highest lord” can be reconciled if the gods were considered his property and he worshipped them in his people’s religion before inviting them to rank him highest.
rows.anchor: فيحسن قولهم ( وآلهتك )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tranquility with God’s remembrance comes from knowing divine unity; trembling comes from fearing deviation from guidance, so the settled believers’ skins first shiver and then soften without contradiction.
rows.anchor: وقد جمع بينهما في قوله ﴿ تقشعر منه جلود الذين يخشون ربهم ثم تلين جلودهم وقلوبهم إلى ذكر الله ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage catalogs occurrences of the forms نزل and أنزل across Qur’anic suras, including Baqara, Al Imran, Nisa, Anam, Araf, Hijr, Nahl, Isra, Furqan, Shuʿara, Ankabut, Saffat, Zumar, Zukhruf, Muhammad, Hadid, and Mulk.
rows.anchor: وفي الزمر ﴿ الله نزل أحسن الحديث ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The catalog notes that the wording “من بعد موتها” occurs in the Qur’an only with the additional preposition min.
rows.anchor: وليس في القرآن ﴿ من بعد موتها ﴾ بزياده من غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition ب can be added to the subject of كفى; “كفى بالله” means “Allah suffices.” Al-Zajjaj explains it as كفى taking on the sense of اكتفى, which the author finds sound.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج دخلت لتضمن كفى معنى اكتفى وهو حسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ can be added to an object even though the verb takes it directly, as in “do not cast yourselves,” “shake the trunk,” and “does he not know that God sees?”
rows.anchor: وفي المفعول نحو ﴿ ولا تلقوا بأيديكم إلى التهلكة ﴾

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Two readings of the bāʾ in “ولا تلقوا بأيديكم” are that ألقي carries the sense of أفضى, or that the phrase means do not cast yourselves to ruin through your own hands, like ruining a matter by one’s judgment.
rows.anchor: وقيل في الأول ضمن تلقوا معنى تفضوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the bāʾ in “تنبت بالدهن” is augmentative, giving the sense “it grows the oil.”
rows.anchor: وقيل في قوله تعالى ﴿ تنبت بالدهن ﴾ 3 إن الباء زائدة والمراد

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh treats the bāʾ in “بأيكم المفتون” as augmentative; Abu al-Hasan instead connects بأيكم to an omitted predicate, with readings of المفتون as a verbal noun or bāʾ as locative.
rows.anchor: وفي المبتدأ وهو قليل ومنه عند سيبويه ﴿ بأيكم المفتون ﴾

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abu al-Hasan treats the bāʾ in “جزاء سيئة بمثلها” as augmentative, supported by the parallel wording “جزاء سيئة سيئة مثلها.”
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الحسن الباء زائدة بدليل قوله في موضع آخر

rows.speaker: ابن عصفور
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAsfur says bāʾ is exceptionally augmentative in a rare, non-analogical construction such as “بقادر”; the author identifies the intended verse and cites its parallel without bāʾ as evidence.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عصفور في المقرب 9 وتزاد في نادر كلام لا يقاس عليه

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj rejects the preceding construction by invoking the prohibition on swearing by other than God; the author calls this objection strange because that prohibition concerns created beings.
rows.anchor: رده الزجاج بالنهي عن الحلف بغير الله وهو عجيب فان ذلك على المخلوقين

rows.speaker: ابن الدهان
rows.claim: For “and those you do not provide for,” Ibn al-Dahhan supplies an implied verb, “and He provides for those you do not.”
rows.anchor: كابن الدهان بتقدير ويرزق من لستم والزجاج بتقدير

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj instead supplies “I mean those you do not provide for”; Abu al-Baqa also construes the phrase as those whom God has provided for, including servants and animals created for people’s benefit.
rows.anchor: والزجاج بتقدير أعني من لستم قال أبو البقاء ( 9 ) لان المعنى اغناكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Masjid al-Haram coordinates with “the way of God” in 2:217, supported by the parallel “they barred you from the Sacred Mosque”; the author notes the intervening كفر is awkward and rejects attachment to “the month” or an unfinished مصدر.
rows.anchor: لان ﴿ المسجد ﴾ معطوف على ﴿ سبيل الله ﴾ في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For حسبك الله ومن اتبعك, the author rejects coordinating من with the genitive pronoun on ك and reads the wāw as accompaniment, with من in the accusative syntactic position, as in the cited verse of poetry.
rows.anchor: ورد بأن الواو للمصاحبة ومن في محل نصب عطف على الموضع

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: On the majority reading, أشد is genitive and coordinates with ذكركم under the comparison kāf, understood as “or like your remembrance, more intense”; this makes remembrance itself a metaphorical remembrance and avoids coordination on a genitive pronoun, forbidden on Hamza’s reading.
rows.anchor: وجعلوه مجرورا عطفا على ﴿ ذكركم ﴾ المجرور بكاف التشبيه

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Most grammarians prohibit coordination on two different governors; al-Akhfash allows it and cites a construction with آيات governed by إن and اختلاف governed by the preposition, but the reply makes آيات emphatic of the earlier word.
rows.anchor: منعه الجمهور واجازه الأخفش محتجا بقوله تعالى ﴿ واختلاف الليل والنهار ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer “Say: O God, Creator of the heavens and earth” is a parenthesis interrupting the passage from people recoiling at mention of God to their claim when relief comes.
rows.anchor: وقوله ﴿ قل اللهم فاطر السماوات والأرض ﴾ 3 إلى قوله ﴿ وحاق بهم ما كانوا به يستهزؤون ﴾ اعتراض في أثناء الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The harmed polytheist’s turning to God contradicts his recoil from divine unity, so the fa-linked clause exposes his inconsistency; the intervening material is separated from the causal connection and joined by wāw for general coordination.
rows.anchor: وذلك لأن قوله ﴿ فإذا مس الإنسان ضر ﴾ سبب عن قوله ﴿ وإذا ذكر الله وحده اشمأزت ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The declaration that God created everything and holds heaven-and-earth’s keys interrupts the connected contrast between the righteous being saved and the disbelievers losing; this follows the Qur’anic pattern of placing opposites in succession.
rows.anchor: وهو على مهيع أسلوب القرآن من ذكر الضد عقب الضد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One classification says the Qur’an contains command, prohibition, report, and question; another lists the Sunna and adds promise and threat.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره القرآن يشتمل على أربعة أنواع من العلوم أمر ونهى وخبر واستخبار

rows.speaker: محمد بن جرير الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari groups the Qur’an’s contents as monotheism, reports, and religious laws; a prophetic report says al-Ikhlas equals one third of the Qur’an because it encompasses monotheism.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن جرير الطبرى يشتمل على ثلاثة أشياء التوحيد والأخبار والديانات

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: Ali b. Isa enumerates thirty kinds of Qur’anic content, including warnings, commands, descriptions of Paradise and Hell, divine attributes and favors, argument, moral contrasts, wisdom, praise of the righteous, and blame of the wicked.
rows.anchor: وقال على بن عيسى القرآن يشتمل على ثلاثين شيئا الإعلام والتنبيه والأمر والنهى

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو المعالي
rows.claim: Abu al-Maʿali says al-Tabari’s three categories encompass the thirty and more; Qur’anic wonders cannot be exhausted, as the verse about God’s keys of the unseen indicates.
rows.anchor: قال القاضى أبو المعالى عزيزى وعلى التحقيق أن تلك الثلاثة التى قالها محمد بن جرير تشمل هذه كلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another classification of Qur’anic word sciences has four: iʿrab, nazm, morphology, and iʿtibar, which serves as the measure of the first three and enables inference.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره علوم ألفاظ القرآن أربعة الإعراب وهو فى الخبر والنظم وهوالقصد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nazm can make an implicit meaning emerge through an apparent wording: “those who have not menstruated” carries a deeper construction, and the question about who begins creation is answered by “God begins creation.”
rows.anchor: والنظم وهوالقصد نحو ﴿ واللائي لم يحضن ﴾ معنى باطن نظم بمعنى ظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Morphology distinguishes related word forms such as أقسط (act justly) and قسط (act unjustly), and بعد (be distant) versus بعد (perish).
rows.anchor: والتصريف فى الكلمة كأقسط عدل وقسط جار وبعد ضد قرب وبعد هلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iʿtibar means seeking clarification and supports inference: the exile of Banu Nadir shows expulsion is a severe punishment and “first gathering” implies later ones; the text also notes their surprise and God’s decree of exile in place of punishment.
rows.anchor: وبه يكون الاستنباط والاستدلال وهو كثير منه ما يعرف بفحوى الكلام
